content: Children currently lack sufficient access to tuberculosis preventive treatment (TPT) options. In the short term, national programs could consider scaling up the use of a three-month regimen of daily rifampicin and isoniazid (3HR) for TB prevention across all pediatric age groups. For children weighing less than 25 kg, including those under 2 years of age, the same fixed-dose combination (FDC) of rifampicin and isoniazid (R/H, 75/50 mg) used in the continuation phase of TB treatment may be administered. Children weighing more than 25 kg may receive either a three-month weekly regimen of rifapentine and isoniazid (3HP) if it is implemented for adults or 3HR using adult FDCs of rifampicin and isoniazid. Child-friendly FDCs of rifampicin and isoniazid offer the added advantage of already being integrated into national supply chains for treating children weighing less than 25 kg. For children on protease inhibitors or integrase inhibitors (e.g., lopinavir/ritonavir, dolutegravir, or nevirapine-based antiretroviral therapy), a six-month isoniazid regimen may be used. However, due to potential drug-drug interactions, careful monitoring for signs of isoniazid-induced hepatitis is necessary. With the use of 3HR in adults, the risk of hepatotoxicity is expected to be comparable to that of sixor nine-month isoniazid regimens (6H/9H). Therefore, 3HP may be a preferred option due to its shorter duration and higher treatment completion rates, which make it more cost-effective in the long term. Over the medium to long term, 3HP (or one month of daily rifapentine and isoniazid, 1HP) may become the preferred regimen across all age groups, provided that appropriate dosing for children under 2 years of age, as well as safety and tolerability, are established. The availability of dispersible FDC formulations of rifapentine and isoniazid will further facilitate this transition. In the meantime, 3HR remains a viable option for young children. Importantly, 3HR should be prioritized as a TPT option for children, given the availability of child-friendly dispersible FDCs that are already in use for TB treatment. The 3HP or 1HP regimens may become the preferred options once data on appropriate dosing across all age groups and the availability of both adult and child-friendly FDC formulations are established. These regimens offer the advantage of once-weekly or one-month medication schedules, which improve adherence and reduce the treatment burden. However, the use of 3HP is currently recommended only for children aged 2 years and older due to limited pharmacokinetic and safety data for children under 2 years of age. Similarly, the suitability of 1HP for children under 13 years of age requires further evaluation based on forthcoming pharmacokinetic and safety studies. Rifampicin-containing FDCs are widely used for treating drug-susceptible TB, but single-dose rifampicin is less commonly procured and may only be available in limited quantities for national programs. If the four-month daily rifampicin regimen (4R) is chosen, the demand for loose tablets of rifampicin will increase, necessitating the identification of quality-assured suppliers. The use of rifampicin should be regulated to prevent its diversion as a broad-spectrum antibiotic. Child-friendly dispersible FDCs of 3HR are already available and widely used in many countries for treating TB disease in children, and these formulations can also be used for TPT. FDCs should be preferred over single pills to reduce the pill burden. For rifapentine, the only currently available formulation is the 150 mg single tablet, which results in a high pill burden for both 3HP and 1HP regimens in adults. Development of 3HP FDCs with a one-to-one ratio of rifapentine and isoniazid is underway, with adult formulations expected to become available soon. This will reduce the pill burden for 3HP in adults from nine to three pills. Similarly, child-friendly 3HP FDC formulations, when available, will reduce the pill burden for children. Further research is needed to define the appropriate dose of rifapentine and identify drug-drug interactions (e.g., with dolutegravir) in children under 2 years of age to facilitate the use of 3HP and 1HP in this age group. Pyridoxine (vitamin B6) supplementation is essential for individuals at risk of peripheral neuropathy, a side effect of long-term high-dose isoniazid therapy. At-risk groups include those with malnutrition, chronic alcohol dependence, HIV infection, renal failure, diabetes, or those who are pregnant or breastfeeding. The standard prophylactic dose of pyridoxine for preventing neuropathy in patients taking isoniazid is 10–25 mg/day. Peripheral neuropathy is infrequent among patients taking standard doses of isoniazid and is usually reversible upon withdrawal of isoniazid and initiation of high-dose pyridoxine therapy (100–200 mg/day). Routine pyridoxine supplementation may not be necessary for otherwise healthy individuals receiving standard-dose isoniazid, and its absence should not delay TPT initiation. In cases of established isoniazid-induced peripheral neuropathy, pyridoxine should be administered at therapeutic doses. A balanced diet containing 1–2 mg of vitamin B6 daily may protect against isoniazid toxicity. Good dietary sources of vitamin B6 include carrots, spinach, peas, potatoes, milk, cheese, eggs, fish, meat, and fortified flour. For high-risk individuals, a small daily dose of 10–25 mg pyridoxine may be given alongside TPT. Pyridoxine can also be provided as part of vitamin B-complex supplements, especially for those who may have deficiencies in other vitamins.
